s0001.literal: The Changes says, "Observe the patterns of culture to transform the empire"; Confucius said, "How splendid—there are patterns indeed."
s0001.idiomatic: In the Book of Changes we read, "Look upon the patterns of culture and thereby transform the world"; Confucius said, "How radiant its patterns are."

s0002.literal: From Chu and Han downward, men of letters emerged generation after generation; at the bend of the Luo and south of the Yangzi, the current grew ever fuller.
s0002.idiomatic: Since the age of Chu and Han, writers have appeared in every generation; at Luoyang and in the lands south of the Yangzi, the stream of letters has run ever wider.

s0003.literal: All thought to rival creation and match sun and moon in brightness; in great matters they took the canonical documents as their model and aided the kingly way, in small matters they kept literary pattern clear and gave voice to the inner spirit.
s0003.idiomatic: Each sought to equal Heaven and Earth in craft and the sun and moon in brilliance; on the large scale they patterned themselves on the ancient canons to support the royal Way, on the small they refined clear prose to release what lay in the heart.

s0004.literal: As for threading ritual and music, synthesizing human relations, penetrating past and present, and narrating good and evil, nothing surpasses this.
s0004.idiomatic: For threading ritual and music, binding human relations, opening past and present, and telling good from evil, nothing stands higher.

s0005.literal: The Last Ruler succeeded to the enterprise, elegantly valued literary composition, sought the arts on every side, and gathered them in splendid array.
s0005.idiomatic: When the Last Ruler came to the throne he prized fine writing, gathered learning from every quarter, and had brilliance heaped together.

s0006.literal: Whenever ministers submitted memorials or presented rhapsodies and eulogies, he personally examined them; if the wording was skilled, his divine brush rewarded and stimulated them and added to their rank—thus the gentry all knew to urge themselves onward.
s0006.idiomatic: Whenever a subject sent up a memorial or offered a fu or song, he read it himself; if the diction was strong, his own hand praised and promoted the writer and raised his rank—so office-holders everywhere took the hint to strive.

s0007.literal: Those whose fame, position, and literary learning shone prominently are discussed separately according to merit and deeds.
s0007.idiomatic: Men whose names, offices, and letters stood out conspicuously are treated elsewhere, judged by achievement.

s0008.literal: What is compiled here now—Du Zhiwei and others whose learning combined with literature—is complete in this chapter, thus.
s0008.idiomatic: What follows records Du Zhiwei and others who united scholarship with letters, gathered in this chapter.

s0009.literal: Xu Boyang, Zhang Zhengjian, Cai Ning, Ruan Zhuo
s0009.idiomatic: Xu Boyang; Zhang Zhengjian; Cai Ning; Ruan Zhuo

s0011.literal: Du Zhiwei, styled Zida, was a native of Qiantang in Wu commandery.
s0011.idiomatic: Du Zhiwei, style name Zida, came from Qiantang in Wu commandery.

s0012.literal: His family for generations practiced Confucian learning and specialized in the Three Rites.
s0012.idiomatic: For generations his house had pursued Confucian study, with the Three Rites as their specialty.

s0013.literal: His father Gui was a Liang court attendant and was friendly with Jiang Ge of Jiyang, grand master for the bright and pure, and Kong Xiuyuan of Kuaiji, director of the ministry of punishment.
s0013.idiomatic: His father Gui served Liang as a court attendant and was on close terms with Jiang Ge of Jiyang, grand master for the bright and pure, and Kong Xiuyuan of Kuaiji, director of the ministry of punishment.

s0014.literal: Zhiwei in youth was keen and clever, with outstanding talent.
s0014.idiomatic: As a boy Zhiwei was quick and sharp, with gifts beyond his years.

s0015.literal: At age seven he received the Documents and gradually studied the Odes and Rites, gaining a rough mastery of those studies.
s0015.idiomatic: At seven he took up the Documents, then little by little the Odes and Rites, until he had a working grasp of each.

s0016.literal: At fifteen he read widely in literature and history and in ritual precedents and old stories; men of his day called him precocious.
s0016.idiomatic: By fifteen he had ranged through literature and history, ritual usage and antiquities; contemporaries hailed him as early-matured.

s0017.literal: Vice Director Xu Mian once saw his writing and valued its force of brush.
s0017.idiomatic: Vice Director Xu Mian once read his work and prized its vigor of style.

s0020.literal: Collation variant: [Tong]; adopted reading: In year 1, Emperor Wu of Liang went in person to Tongtai Temple to offer his body, and ordered Mian to draft and fix the ritual regulations. Editorial footnote marker 1. Mian said the court had never had this rite before and summoned Zhiwei to draft the ritual in outline.
s0020.idiomatic: Collation variant: [Tong]; adopted reading: In the first year, Emperor Wu of Liang went to Tongtai Temple to "yield his person" in the Buddhist rite and ordered Mian to set down the ceremonial rules. [1] Mian replied that the palace had no precedent for it and called Zhiwei to sketch the forms.

s0021.literal: He was then appointed supplemental eastern-palace academician; with the academicians Liu Zhi and others he copied and compiled from the mass of books, each taking a topic.
s0021.idiomatic: He was soon made a supplemental academician in the eastern palace and, with Liu Zhi and the other academicians, excerpted the libraries, each assigned a theme.

s0022.literal: The two pieces he drafted, "Enriching Instruction" and "The Way of Government," both had prefaces by Zhiwei.
s0022.idiomatic: Of the two treatises he wrote, "Enriching Instruction" and "The Way of Government," Zhiwei supplied the prefaces for both.

s0023.literal: When the Marquis of Xiangyin, Xiao Ang, became inspector of Jiang province, he made Zhiwei master of his secretariat.
s0023.idiomatic: When Xiao Ang, Marquis of Xiangyin, took up the Jiangzhou inspectorate, he put Zhiwei in charge of his secretariat.

s0024.literal: Editorial footnote marker 2. When Ang died, the Prince of Luling, Xu, replaced him; he also sent a personal instruction to summon him, but Zhiwei firmly declined and would not accept the appointment, and instead escorted Ang's coffin back to the capital.
s0024.idiomatic: [2] When Ang died, Xiao Xu of Luling succeeded him and again wrote in his own hand to recruit Zhiwei; Zhiwei refused outright, saw Ang's bier home to the capital, and would not take the post.

s0027.idiomatic: Collation variant: [city]; adopted reading: He continued as companion to the Duke of Lincheng for his lessons.

s0028.literal: Editorial footnote marker 3. Soon he was made staff officer for deliberation in Yang province, secretariat aide to the Prince of Nankang, and concurrent inner-limit erudite of the Imperial University.
s0028.idiomatic: [3] Before long he was made deliberation staff officer in Yangzhou, secretariat aide to the Prince of Nankang, and at the same time an inner-limit erudite of the national university.

s0029.literal: Collation variant: [Datong]; adopted reading: In year 7, Editorial footnote marker 4. the Liang crown prince performed the libation sacrifice to Confucius at the national university; at the time the Music Office had no ascending-song lyrics for Confucius and Yan Hui. Editorial footnote marker 5. The secretariat deliberator ordered Zhiwei to compose the text; the musicians transmitted and practiced it, and it became precedent.
s0029.idiomatic: Collation variant: [Datong]; adopted reading: In the seventh year, [4] the Liang crown prince offered the Confucian libation at the national university. The Music Office then lacked ascending-song words for Confucius and Yan Hui; [5] the secretariat deliberator had Zhiwei write them. The performers learned and kept them, and they became custom.

s0030.literal: He was transferred and made field-office aide to the Prince of Shaoling, then moved to prison-office aide.
s0030.idiomatic: He was reassigned as field-office aide to the Prince of Shaoling, then as prison-office aide.

s0031.literal: Though Zhiwei's age and rank were very low, he was known throughout the age solely for strong memory and outstanding talent; Director of the Ministry of Personnel Zhang Zuan understood him deeply and regarded him as material for the state altar.
s0031.idiomatic: Zhiwei was still young and low in rank, yet his encyclopedic mind and sharp gifts had already made him a name; Personnel Director Zhang Zuan saw him clearly and treated him as a future pillar of the court.

s0032.literal: When Hou Jing rebelled, Zhiwei fled and hid in mountains and marshes.
s0032.idiomatic: When Hou Jing rose in rebellion, Zhiwei hid in the hills and marshes.

s0033.literal: When the Founder became chief minister, he had long heard his name and summoned him as supplemental secretariat aide.
s0033.idiomatic: Once the Founder was chief minister he had long known Zhiwei's reputation and called him in as a supplemental secretariat aide.

s0034.literal: He was moved to palace secretariat gentleman and concurrently headed the grand directorate.
s0034.idiomatic: He was promoted to palace secretariat gentleman and at the same time directed the grand history office.

s0035.literal: When the Founder received the abdication, he was made grand master of splendid felicity; the rest of his posts remained as before.
s0035.idiomatic: When the Founder took the throne he was made grand master of splendid felicity while keeping his other offices.

s0036.literal: Zhiwei memorialized asking to be relieved of the directorate, saying: "Your servant, in Shaotai year 1, was honored as palace secretariat gentleman and has managed the national history for four years to this day.
s0036.idiomatic: Zhiwei asked to resign the history directorship, writing: "In Shaotai year 1 (555) I was undeservedly made palace secretariat gentleman and have kept the national annals for four years now.

s0037.literal: Your servant is by nature base and lowly and was wrongly favored with recognition; I think to repay grace and reward and dare not abandon office.
s0037.idiomatic: I am by nature mean and unworthy, yet was noticed and favored; I wished to repay that kindness and did not dare leave my post.

s0038.literal: The imperial chronology is newly renewed; we are driven before the chariot of heaven—recording words and recording events is not easy to entrust to one man; talent for the directorate should rather be chosen from the many.
s0038.idiomatic: The dynasty is new, the court rides under broad heaven, and to set down speech and deed is work for no single hand; the post of compiler ought to go to worthier men.

s0039.literal: Censor-in-chief Shen Jiong, left vice director Xu Ling, former Liang concurrent grand compiler Yu Li, and former Liang yellow-gate gentleman Kong Huan—some with clear writing and ample brush, some with strong memory and mastery of antiquity—the charge of Sima Qian and Dong Zhongshu truly belongs to this group of talents; your servant has no grounds to rush and change the court and market, Editorial footnote marker 6. and again obstruct the path of the worthy.
s0039.idiomatic: Censor-in-chief Shen Jiong, left vice director Xu Ling, Liang's former concurrent grand compiler Yu Li, and Liang's former yellow-gate gentleman Kong Huan—some write with clarity and fullness, some remember deeply and know the old—are fit for the work of Qian and Dong; I have no excuse to bolt from court again [6] and block better men.

s0040.literal: In Yao's court all yielded—truly not to be pursued; to offer one's strength and take one's place is what I hope may win exemption.
s0040.idiomatic: Even in Yao's time men stepped aside—that cannot be matched now; let me serve where I belong, and perhaps I may be released.

s0041.literal: " A gracious edict did not permit it.
s0041.idiomatic: " The emperor's gracious edict refused him.

s0042.literal: Soon he was moved to grand master of works, promoted to grand master for the palace, and still ordered to compile the History of Liang.
s0042.idiomatic: He was soon made grand master of works, then grand master for the palace, and still charged with compiling the Liang history.

s0043.literal: In Yongding year 3 he died, aged fifty-two.
s0043.idiomatic: In Yongding year 3 (559) he died at fifty-two.

s0044.literal: The Founder deeply mourned and regretted him; an edict posthumously made him direct and upright attendant of the scattered cavalry, granted fifty thousand in funeral money, fifty bolts of cloth, one coffin, and fixed a day for mourning rites.
s0044.idiomatic: The Founder grieved him deeply and ordered him posthumously made direct and upright attendant of the scattered cavalry, with fifty thousand cash in funeral gift, fifty bolts of cloth, one coffin, and a set day for the mourning service.

s0045.literal: Zhiwei in writing did not pursue florid display but was warm, elegant, and broadly ample.
s0045.idiomatic: Zhiwei's prose shunned ornament; it was mild, refined, and rich.

s0046.literal: Much of what he composed was lost; seventeen scrolls survive.
s0046.idiomatic: Most of his writings are gone; seventeen scrolls remain.

s0047.literal: Yan Huang, styled Yuanming, was a native of Linyi in Langye.
s0047.idiomatic: Yan Huang, style name Yuanming, came from Linyi in Langye.

s0048.literal: Orphaned young and poor, he loved learning and had literary grace.
s0048.idiomatic: He lost his father early and grew up poor, yet loved study and had a gift for words.

s0049.literal: On first leaving the sackcloth he was made concurrent secretariat aide to the Prince of Shaoling of Liang.
s0049.idiomatic: On first taking office he became a concurrent secretariat aide on the Prince of Shaoling's staff under Liang.

s0050.literal: At the time the eastern-palace academician Yu Xin was once sent on mission to the prince's establishment; the prince had Huang receive and reply to him. Xin looked down on him for being young and said, "How many concurrent secretariat aides does this establishment have?"
s0050.idiomatic: Once when eastern-palace academician Yu Xin was sent to the prince's house, the prince had Huang answer him. Xin, thinking him too young, asked, "How many concurrent secretariat aides has this establishment, anyway?"

s0051.literal: Huang replied, "Still fewer than the palace academics."
s0051.idiomatic: Huang answered, "Still fewer than the academics inside the palace."

s0052.literal: Men of the time regarded it as a fine retort.
s0052.idiomatic: Contemporaries judged it a sharp reply.

s0053.literal: In Hou Jing's turmoil he fled west to Jing province.
s0053.idiomatic: During Hou Jing's rebellion he fled west to Jingzhou.

s0054.literal: At the beginning of Chengsheng he was made palace secretariat gentleman.
s0054.idiomatic: At the opening of Chengsheng he was appointed palace secretariat gentleman.

s0055.literal: At the time Du Kan was grand administrator of Wuxing and devoted himself solely to valor and force; his district had many reckless young men, and Emperor Yuan was troubled by this, so he had Huang oversee his correspondence.
s0055.idiomatic: Du Kan was then grand administrator of Wuxing and cared only for bold fighting; his commandery teemed with hotheaded youths, which troubled Emperor Yuan, who put Huang in charge of Kan's documents.

s0056.literal: He also instructed Kan: "You are still young; it is not too late to study and read. Yan Huang is a man of letters—have him assist you at your side; in every hurried matter you must consult and report."
s0056.idiomatic: The emperor also told Kan: "You are still young and can still learn. Yan Huang is a literary man—let him stand beside you; even in passing affairs you must ask his counsel."

s0057.literal: When Kan was executed, Huang returned to Emperor Wen; Emperor Wen entrusted him with secretarial records and favored him with great intimacy.
s0057.idiomatic: After Kan was killed, Huang entered Emperor Wen's service; the emperor gave him charge of documents and treated him with exceptional closeness.

s0058.literal: He was made recorder of the Xuanyi establishment and concurrent secretariat aide.
s0058.idiomatic: He was made recorder on the Xuanyi staff and concurrent secretariat aide.

s0059.literal: In Yongding year 2 the Founder visited the Great Zhuangyan Monastery; that night sweet dew descended, and Huang presented a eulogy on the sweet dew whose wording and sense were comprehensive and canonical; the Founder marveled at it greatly.
s0059.idiomatic: In Yongding year 2 (558) the Founder went to the Great Zhuangyan Monastery; sweet dew fell that night, and Huang offered a "Sweet Dew" eulogy, learned and apt in phrasing—the Founder was astonished.

s0060.literal: At the beginning of Tianjia he was moved to supernumerary attendant of the scattered cavalry and concurrent palace secretariat attendant, in charge of edicts and commands.
s0060.idiomatic: Early in Tianjia he rose to supernumerary attendant of the scattered cavalry and concurrent palace secretariat attendant, drafting edicts.

s0061.literal: In year 3 he died, aged fifty-three.
s0061.idiomatic: In Tianjia year 3 (562) he died at fifty-three.

s0062.literal: An edict posthumously made him minister of public works, gave the posthumous title Baron of Integrity, and granted a burial plot as well.
s0062.idiomatic: He was posthumously made minister of public works, titled Baron of Integrity, and given a grave plot besides.

s0063.literal: Huang's family for generations was a single gate without collateral kin on either side, yet he stood apart and cultivated himself and was known to the age.
s0063.idiomatic: His house was a lone branch without kin to lean on, yet he held himself upright and won notice in his time.

s0064.literal: His memorials and edict drafts were finished the moment the brush touched paper and at once hit the matter's core, yet were elegant in spirit.
s0064.idiomatic: Memorials and edicts from his hand came whole as soon as he wrote and always struck the point, yet kept a noble tone.

s0065.literal: He left a collection in twenty scrolls.
s0065.idiomatic: A collection of twenty scrolls survives.

s0069.literal: Collation variant: [Decao]; styled Decao, Editorial footnote marker 7. a native of Kaocheng in Jiyang.
s0069.idiomatic: Collation variant: [Decao]; styled Decao, [7] from Kaocheng in Jiyang.

s0070.literal: His grandfather Rouzhi was a Qi director in the ministry of revenue's granaries section.
s0070.idiomatic: His grandfather Rouzhi had been a Qi director in the granaries section of the revenue ministry.

s0071.literal: His father Ge was Liang director of revenue and grand master for the bright and pure.
s0071.idiomatic: His father Ge served Liang as director of revenue and grand master for the bright and pure.

s0072.literal: Decao loved learning and was skilled at composition.
s0072.idiomatic: Decao loved study and wrote well.

s0073.literal: His bearing was fine; he stood seven chi four cun in height.
s0073.idiomatic: He was handsome in bearing, seven chi four cun tall.

s0074.literal: By nature he was utmost in filial piety and served his parents with full ritual.
s0074.idiomatic: He was deeply filial and waited on his parents with complete propriety.

s0075.literal: He lived with half-brothers of a different mother and was very generous and affectionate among them.
s0075.idiomatic: He dwelt with uterine brothers and was warm and generous toward them.

s0076.literal: On first taking office he was a traveling aide on the staff of the Prince of Wuling, southern army lieutenant of the center.
s0076.idiomatic: He began as a traveling aide on the Prince of Wuling's staff in the southern army of the center.

s0077.literal: Grand marshal the Prince of Nanping, Xiao Wei, heard of his talent and summoned him as eastern-pavilion libationer.
s0077.idiomatic: Grand Marshal Xiao Wei, Prince of Nanping, heard of his gifts and made him eastern-pavilion libationer.

s0078.literal: He was moved to outer-army aide on the Prince of Xiangdong's western staff, then made director in the ministry of punishment's comparison section, and left office on his father's mourning.
s0078.idiomatic: He was transferred to outer-army aide on the western staff of the Prince of Xiangdong, then made a comparison-section director in the ministry of punishment, and resigned when his father died.

s0079.literal: After the mourning period ended, his appearance was wasted and emaciated as if still in mourning.
s0079.idiomatic: When mourning was over he was still gaunt and worn, as though the coffin had not long left the house.

s0080.literal: He was made secretariat master to the Prince of Wuling of the western army but did not take up the post.
s0080.idiomatic: He was appointed secretariat master to the Prince of Wuling on the western army staff but declined.

s0081.literal: After a long while he was appointed secretariat aide to the Prince of Luling.
s0081.idiomatic: Only after a long interval was he made secretariat aide to the Prince of Luling.

s0082.literal: He was made director of the Court of Judicial Review, then went out as senior aide of Nanzhou.
s0082.idiomatic: He became director of the Court of Judicial Review, then left the capital as senior aide of South Xuzhou.

s0083.literal: When the Founder was minister of works and general who campaigns north, he brought Decao in as staff deliberator.
s0083.idiomatic: When the Founder was minister of works and northern campaign general, he drew Decao in as a staff deliberator.

s0084.literal: He was moved to palace secretariat gentleman and promoted to chief clerk to the Prince of Linhai of the cloud-banners guard.
s0084.idiomatic: He was promoted to palace secretariat gentleman, then chief clerk to the Prince of Linhai in the cloud-banners guard.

s0085.literal: When the Chen court was established, he was appointed vice director in the ministry of personnel.
s0085.idiomatic: When Chen was founded he was made vice director in the ministry of personnel.

s0086.literal: When the Founder received the abdication, he was made director of the secretariat and concurrently left vice director in the Masters of Writing.
s0086.idiomatic: At the Founder's accession he became director of the secretariat and concurrently left vice director in the Masters of Writing.

s0087.literal: Soon, in his original office, he was additionally made palace secretariat attendant.
s0087.idiomatic: Shortly afterward he was also made palace secretariat attendant while keeping his prior post.

s0088.literal: In Tianjia year 4 he was additionally made attendant of the scattered cavalry and, with palace secretariat gentleman Liu Shizhi, was sent as envoy to Qi; Editorial footnote marker 8. he composed Record of the Roads of the Northern Expedition in three scrolls.
s0088.idiomatic: In Tianjia year 4 (563) he was further made attendant of the scattered cavalry and, with Liu Shizhi of the palace secretariat, went on embassy to Qi; [8] he wrote Record of the Roads of the Northern Expedition in three scrolls.

s0089.literal: On return he was made junior mentor to the crown prince and concurrently colonel of footsoldiers.
s0089.idiomatic: Back home he was appointed junior mentor to the heir apparent and colonel of footsoldiers.

s0090.literal: Before long he was moved to censor-in-chief and was dismissed for a public-service offense.
s0090.idiomatic: Soon he was made censor-in-chief, then removed for a fault in office.

s0091.literal: Soon he was appointed general who shakes the distance and direct and upright attendant of the scattered cavalry.
s0091.idiomatic: He was soon restored as general who shakes the distance and direct and upright attendant of the scattered cavalry.

s0092.literal: He asked on his own to govern a county and went out as magistrate of Xinyu; his government prized kindness and favor and achieved notable results unlike others.
s0092.idiomatic: He sought a county post of his own accord and was sent out as magistrate of Xinyu, ruling with grace and leaving an unusual record.

s0093.literal: In year 6 he died in office, aged fifty-seven.
s0093.idiomatic: In the sixth year he died in his post at fifty-seven.

s0094.literal: Emperor Wen deeply mourned and regretted him; an edict posthumously made him attendant of the scattered cavalry.
s0094.idiomatic: Emperor Wen grieved him deeply and posthumously made him attendant of the scattered cavalry.

s0095.literal: Literary works he authored fill fifteen scrolls.

s0096.literal: His son Chun was also skilled at composition and served as junior mentor to the heir apparent and left vice director in the Masters of Writing.
s0096.idiomatic: His son Chun also wrote well and rose to junior mentor to the heir apparent and left vice director in the Masters of Writing.

s0097.literal: Yu Chi, styled Yunde, Editorial footnote marker 9. was a native of Yanling in Yingchuan.
s0097.idiomatic: Yu Chi, style name Yunde, [9] came from Yanling in Yingchuan.

s0098.literal: His grandfather Peiyu was Song interior governor of Changsha.
s0098.idiomatic: His grandfather Peiyu had been Song interior governor of Changsha.

s0099.literal: His father Collation variant: [Sha] Mi, Editorial footnote marker 10. was a Liang magistrate of Changcheng.
s0099.idiomatic: His father, collation variant: [Sha] Mi, [10] had been magistrate of Changcheng under Liang.

s0100.literal: Chi was orphaned young; by nature he was utmost in filial piety and in mourning his father exceeded the rites.
s0100.idiomatic: Chi lost his father early, was deeply filial by nature, and in mourning went beyond the prescribed rites.
